Your response was: "I mean... I looked through it. There were some parts that felt familiar, some that didn't quite. I'm not sure I'm the right person to say whether it all makes sense — it depends a lot on who would normally use this. I suppose some things stuck with me a bit more than others — there was more than one option, I think, near the middle of the screen, and I wasn't quite sure which one was the main one. Something about the way the options were presented felt a bit mixed up to me. I couldn't say much more than that without thinking about it more."

We want to understand what you meant by "something about the way the options were presented felt a bit mixed up to me", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The visual hierarchy of the buttons seems reversed, with the dark "Continue Shopping" button appearing more prominent than the light grey "Place Order" button.
B) The vertical placement of the buttons feels counter-intuitive, as the option to leave ("Continue Shopping") is stacked above the option to complete the purchase ("Place Order").
C) The two action buttons are presented as equal-sized blocks at the bottom without clear visual distinction, making it hard to tell which one is the primary next step.
D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to)

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
turns.a: A) The visual hierarchy of the buttons seems reversed, with the dark "Continue Shopping" button appearing more prominent than the light grey "Place Order" button.

turns.q: What kind of work situation usually brings you to a screen where you need to assess the priority between continuing versus placing an order?
turns.a: I suppose just... complete the transaction. Confirm the order. I don't usually think of it as a 'job' — it's more like the last step in something larger. Getting it over the line without any detours.

turns.q: What specific information about the order confirmation process were you hoping to see confirmed when you noticed the dark "Continue Shopping" button visually outweighing the lighter "Place Order" button?
turns.a: I'd know it worked if... nothing went sideways. If the right choice registered and a confirmation appeared — not a shopping page. That's what success looks like here. Not being sent somewhere unexpected.

turns.q: How should the contrast between these buttons look to make it immediately clear that placing the order is the intended action here?
turns.a: 'Place Order' should look like a filled button in a distinct color — the kind that reads as 'this is the final step.' Right now they don't communicate that difference at all. That's the only fix needed.

turns.q: When you look at the "Place Order" button in this layout, what specific visual property—like its fill type, color shade, contrast level, or border style—makes it fail to stand out as the primary action?
turns.a: 'Continue Shopping' was styled as if it were the main action — more visual weight, more presence on the page than I'd expect for a button that takes you backward. 'Place Order' — the actual thing I needed to do — looked secondary by comparison. That's the barrier. The fix: downgrade 'Continue Shopping' to a ghost button or a text link, something that reads as optional. And give 'Place Order' a solid fill color with real contrast so it's unmistakably the primary action. If those two things were right — 'Continue Shopping' quiet, 'Place Order' prominent — I'd have known immediately which was the right one without any hesitation.
